blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Model selection is choosing which predictors, and in what form, enter a final regression model. Overfitting is what happens when a model has too many parameters for the data: it fits the noise of this sample as well as the signal, so it describes this sample better than it will describe the next one.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A model with too few predictors misses real relationships. A model with too many learns the quirks of one sample. Figure 15.1 shows the pattern: as predictors are added, the error in the data used to fit the model keeps falling, but the error in new data eventually rises again. The tools in this section, likelihood (§15.1.1), AIC and BIC (§15.1.2), stepwise search (§15.1.3) and the likelihood ratio test (§15.1.4), all try to find the turning point. §15.1.5 then explains why the right tool depends on what the model is for.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: With 30 candidate predictors and 100 observations, a model containing all 30 can reproduce the sample closely and still predict new patients badly: it has spent its information on idiosyncrasies of these 100 people.

blocks.alt: Training error and test error as model complexity increases
blocks.caption: Figure 15.1. Schematic: error in the data used for fitting (training error) falls steadily as predictors are added; error in new data (test error) falls, then rises once the model starts fitting noise.

points.html: Underfitting (too few predictors) and overfitting (too many) are the two failure modes; selection tools balance them.
Statistical criteria never replace subject knowledge about which variables are plausible confounders or predictors (§15.1.5).

blocks.html: Model Fit and the Idea of Likelihood

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Recall from §13.1 that the likelihood L of a set of parameter values is the probability of the observed data calculated as if those values were true, and that maximum likelihood chooses the values that make L as large as possible. The maximised log-likelihood, ln L, is a measure of model fit: the less negative it is, the better the model fits the data it was fitted to. The deviance is −2 ln L (up to a constant that is the same for every model fitted to the same data): lower deviance means better fit.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: R² (recall §12.2.5) measures fit by squared residuals, and it can only rise when a predictor is added. Log-likelihood works for every model fitted by maximum likelihood (logistic, Poisson; Cox regression uses a closely related partial likelihood) and has exactly the same weakness: adding a predictor, even pure noise, never lowers the maximised likelihood. So raw fit cannot choose between models of different sizes. A fair comparison needs a penalty that grows with the number of parameters (§15.1.2) or a formal test of whether the extra parameters earn their place (§15.1.4).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why an extra predictor can never lower the maximised likelihood. Let model A have coefficients b₀, b₁, and model B add b₂.

  1. Model B with b₂ set to 0 is exactly model A, so it can reach A’s maximum likelihood, L_A.
  2. Maximum likelihood for B searches over all values of b₂, including 0.
  3. So L_B ≥ L_A, with equality only if the best b₂ is exactly 0.

In a real sample the best b₂ for a noise variable is almost never exactly 0, so ln L rises a little.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the CBHI survey (recall the membership model of §13.3), membership modelled on distance and wealth gives ln L = −276.13. Adding maternal education (two more coefficients) raises it to −273.58. Adding household size as well, a variable with no detectable association with membership (crude p = 0.56), still nudges it up, to −273.57.

points.html: ln L measures fit for any maximum-likelihood model; deviance = −2 ln L.
A bigger model never fits its own sample worse (the Derivation). So fit alone cannot choose model size.

blocks.html: AIC and BIC

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
For a model with k estimated parameters (including the intercept), fitted to n observations:

AIC = −2 ln L + 2k

BIC = −2 ln L + k × ln n

These are the Akaike and Bayesian (Schwarz) information criteria (formulas as documented in R; R Core Team). The penalty is added to the deviance, so lower is better. The derivations of the two penalties (from information theory and from an approximation to Bayesian model comparison) are beyond this book.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The first term, −2 ln L, falls as fit improves. The second term rises by 2 (AIC) or by ln n (BIC) for every parameter added. A new parameter lowers AIC only if it lowers the deviance by more than 2. BIC’s penalty per parameter, ln n, exceeds AIC’s 2 whenever ln n > 2, that is, n ≥ 8 (e² = 7.39). In any realistic study BIC therefore penalises size more heavily and tends to choose smaller models.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Three CBHI membership models, all fitted to the same 500 households: A (distance, wealth), B (A + maternal education, 2 parameters), C (B + household size).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Model A: k = 3, ln L = −276.13, deviance = 552.25. AIC = 552.25 + 2 × 3 = 558.25. BIC = 552.25 + 3 × ln 500 = 552.25 + 3 × 6.215 = 570.90.
  2. Model B: k = 5, deviance = 547.16. AIC = 547.16 + 10 = 557.16. BIC = 547.16 + 5 × 6.215 = 578.24.
  3. Model C: k = 6, deviance = 547.15. AIC = 547.15 + 12 = 559.15. BIC = 547.15 + 6 × 6.215 = 584.43.
  4. AIC prefers B (lowest, 557.16). BIC prefers A (570.90). Education lowers the deviance by 5.09 for 2 parameters: more than AIC’s price of 4, less than BIC’s price of 12.43.
  5. Both reject C: household size lowers the deviance by 0.02, far less than either price.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
cb$maternal_education <- factor(cb$maternal_education,
  levels = c("none", "primary", "secondary+"))
mA <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index,
          family = binomial, data = cb)
mB <- update(mA, . ~ . + maternal_education)
mC <- update(mB, . ~ . + household_size)
sapply(list(A = mA, B = mB, C = mC), function(m)
  round(c(k = attr(logLik(m), "df"), lnL = as.numeric(logLik(m)),
          AIC = AIC(m), BIC = BIC(m)), 2))
anova(mA, mB, test = "LRT")
          A       B       C
k      3.00    5.00    6.00
lnL -276.13 -273.58 -273.57
AIC  558.25  557.16  559.15
BIC  570.90  578.24  584.43
Analysis of Deviance Table

Model 1: cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index
Model 2: cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index + maternal_education
  Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi)  
1       497     552.25                       
2       495     547.16  2   5.0895  0.07849 .

logLik gives ln L and its df attribute gives k; AIC and BIC reproduce the hand calculations. The second block is the likelihood ratio test of §15.1.4: the drop in deviance (5.09) on 2 df.

points.html: AIC = −2 ln L + 2k; BIC = −2 ln L + k ln n. Penalty added, lower is better.
BIC penalises more than AIC once n ≥ 8, so it favours smaller models. When they disagree, as here, the data do not strongly favour either model.
A lower AIC means a better fit-versus-complexity trade-off among the candidates compared, not a true or even a good model.
Compare AIC or BIC only between models fitted to the same outcome and exactly the same observations. A variable with missing values silently drops rows and makes the comparison invalid.
k counts parameters, not variables: a three-level categorical predictor adds 2.

blocks.html: Stepwise Selection

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Stepwise selection adds or removes predictors one at a time by a fixed rule, a p-value threshold or a fall in AIC, until no single change improves the criterion. Forward selection starts empty and adds; backward elimination starts full and removes; bidirectional does both.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Stepwise selection is a search procedure; AIC, BIC or a p-value is the scoring rule it follows. It is quick and automatic, and that is the problem: it has no subject knowledge, it answers a different question in every sample, and the p-values and confidence intervals it reports for the survivors ignore the search that produced them. A review of variable selection concludes that selection, “in particular if used in explanatory modeling where effect estimates are of central interest, can compromise stability of a final model, unbiasedness of regression coefficients, and validity of p-values or confidence intervals” (Heinze, Wallisch & Dunkler, 2018). Treat stepwise output as a warning sign, not a method.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Backward elimination from model C (§15.1.2) with the AIC penalty keeps distance, wealth and education (model B). With the BIC penalty it keeps only distance and wealth (model A). Same data, same procedure, different answer, because the scoring rule changed.

To see the instability, repeat the AIC search in 200 bootstrap samples (samples of 500 households drawn with replacement from the 500; the resampling idea of §7.2.4). Distance is kept in 96.5% of samples and wealth in 100%, but education only in 69.5%, and household size, which shows no detectable association with membership, still enters 15.5% of the final models.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
# cb as in §15.1.2
full <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index +
              maternal_education + household_size,
            family = binomial, data = cb)
# AIC penalty (k = 2)
formula(step(full, trace = 0))
# BIC penalty (k = ln n)
formula(step(full, trace = 0, k = log(500)))
# how stable is the AIC choice?
set.seed(2026)
keep <- replicate(200, {
  b <- cb[sample(500, replace = TRUE), ]
  s <- step(update(full, data = b), trace = 0)
  vars <- c("distance_km", "wealth_index", "maternal_education",
            "household_size")
  vars %in% attr(terms(s), "term.labels")
})
setNames(rowMeans(keep),
         c("distance", "wealth", "education", "household size"))
cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index + maternal_education
cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index
      distance         wealth      education household size 
         0.965          1.000          0.695          0.155

step drops terms while AIC falls; k = log(500) turns the penalty into BIC’s. The last line is the share of bootstrap samples whose final model kept each variable: an honest report of how much the “selected model” depends on the sample.

points.html: Stepwise selection is a search; the criterion (p-value, AIC, BIC) decides its answer.
Known problems: unstable choices, inflated apparent significance, and p-values and CIs that ignore the selection (Heinze et al., 2018).
Do not use it to choose confounders: confounder status is a causal question (recall §11.6.1), which no p-value or fit statistic can settle.
If selection is unavoidable, report inclusion frequencies across bootstrap samples, as above (Heinze et al., 2018).

blocks.html: Likelihood Ratio Test

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The likelihood ratio test (LRT) compares two nested models: the reduced model is the full model with some parameters fixed at 0. It tests H₀: those extra parameters are all 0. The statistic is

LR = −2 × (ln L_reduced − ln L_full) = deviance_reduced − deviance_full

Under H₀, LR follows approximately a χ² distribution (recall §5.7.2.4) with df = the difference in the number of estimated parameters. The approximation is a large-sample result (Wilks’ theorem; proof beyond this book).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: AIC and BIC score models; the LRT is a hypothesis test (recall Chapter 8). The Derivation in §15.1.1 guarantees that LR ≥ 0. The question is whether the gain in fit is bigger than chance alone would produce with that many extra parameters. Nesting matters: every parameter of the reduced model must be in the full model, and both must use the same observations. The df counts parameters, not variables: adding maternal education (three levels) adds 2 parameters and 2 df.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: §13.3 fitted the CBHI membership model with education. Does education, as a whole, add to distance and wealth?

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. ln L_reduced (model A) = −276.126; ln L_full (model B) = −273.581.
  2. LR = −2 × (−276.126 + 273.581) = −2 × (−2.545) = 5.09.
  3. df = 5 − 3 = 2 (two education coefficients).
  4. p = P(χ²₂ > 5.09) = 0.078. For 2 df the χ² upper tail is exactly e^(−x/2), so p = e^(−2.545) = 0.078.
  5. Conclusion: weak evidence that maternal education adds to distance and wealth. Note the contrast with §13.3, where the single coefficient for secondary education had p = 0.027. The LRT asks a different question (both education coefficients together, 2 df) and spends its evidence on both.

points.html: LR = −2(ln L_reduced − ln L_full); χ² with df = difference in the number of parameters; approximate, large-sample.
Only for nested models fitted to the same observations. For non-nested models, use AIC or BIC.
For a multi-level categorical variable, the LRT (joint test) is the right test of “does this variable matter?”, not the p-value of any one level.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.1

questions.prompt: A colleague says, “Model B has lower AIC than model A, so model B is the true model.” What is the overstatement?
questions.answer: AIC ranks only the candidates actually compared. A lower AIC means B has the better fit-versus-complexity trade-off of the two, judged by −2 ln L + 2k on these data. It says nothing about whether B is correct, causally meaningful, or even a good model: both candidates could be poor, and a model not considered could be better. With a small AIC difference (as in §15.1.2, 557.16 against 558.25) the data barely prefer one over the other, and BIC may disagree.

questions.prompt: Why does adding a purely random predictor never lower a model’s maximised likelihood? Give the argument, not just the conclusion.
questions.answer: The larger model contains the smaller one: setting the new coefficient to 0 reproduces the smaller model exactly, with the same likelihood. Maximum likelihood for the larger model searches over all values of that coefficient, including 0, so its maximum can only be equal to or higher than the smaller model’s. In a real sample the best value of the new coefficient is almost never exactly 0 (chance alignment with noise), so the likelihood rises slightly. This is why raw fit cannot choose model size and a penalty or a test is needed.

questions.prompt: A logistic model on 400 children has ln L = −210.4 with 4 parameters. Adding a four-category feeding-practice variable gives ln L = −205.9. Compute the LR statistic, its df, the change in AIC and the change in BIC. Which criteria favour the larger model?
questions.answer:
1. LR = −2 × (−210.4 − (−205.9)) = −2 × (−4.5) = 9.0.
  2. A four-category variable adds 3 parameters, so df = 3. p = P(χ²₃ > 9.0) = 0.029.
  3. ΔAIC = (change in −2 ln L) + 2 × 3 = −9.0 + 6 = −3.0: AIC falls, so AIC favours the larger model.
  4. ΔBIC = −9.0 + 3 × ln 400 = −9.0 + 3 × 5.99 = −9.0 + 17.97 = +8.97: BIC rises, so BIC favours the smaller model.
  5. The LRT (p = 0.029) and AIC favour adding feeding practice; BIC, with its heavier penalty, does not.

blocks.html: Modelling Strategy – Explanatory, Predictive and Descriptive Aims

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A modelling strategy is the plan, fixed before the analysis, for which variables enter a model and in what form. It follows from the model’s aim:

  • Explanatory (causal): estimate the effect of one exposure on an outcome, free of confounding.
  • Predictive: predict the outcome for new individuals as accurately as possible.
  • Descriptive: summarise how the outcome is distributed across groups, without a causal or predictive claim.

Shmueli (2010) argues that “conflation between explanation and prediction is common, yet the distinction must be understood”, because the two aims lead to different choices at every step of modelling.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Explanatory models are built from a causal diagram (recall §11.6.1). Draw the DAG, find a sufficient adjustment set by the backdoor criterion, and put those variables in the model whether or not they are “significant”. Do not adjust for mediators or colliders. The coefficient of interest is one number, the exposure’s; the other coefficients are there to remove confounding and should not be interpreted as effects in their own right. Check that the data can support the model: the events-per-variable convention (recall §13.2.4) limits how many parameters you can afford.

Predictive models choose variables for accuracy in new data. Causal structure does not matter; a variable that is a consequence of the outcome’s causes can be a good predictor. What matters is not overfitting: prefer a pre-specified set of predictors chosen from the literature, penalised methods that shrink coefficients towards 0 (shrinkage: pulling estimates towards 0 to offset overfitting), and honest validation in data not used for fitting. §15.5.2 (validating clinical prediction models by discrimination and calibration) develops this.

Descriptive models report, for example, prevalence of anaemia by district and wealth quintile. They should be pre-specified and interpreted as associations only.

Two habits to drop.

  1. Univariable p-value screening (keeping only variables with p < 0.05 or 0.20 in a crude analysis). It “wrongly rejects potentially important variables when the relationship between an outcome and a risk factor is confounded” (Sun, Shook & Kay, 1996): a crude association can be hidden by confounding and appear only after adjustment.
  2. Stepwise selection for explanatory models (§15.1.3). It chooses variables by their association with the outcome, not by their causal role.

Form matters as well as choice. Keep continuous variables continuous, and model curvature with categories, a trend test or splines rather than cut-points (recall §12.4.5).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Three questions from the same CBHI survey:

Aim Question Strategy
Explanatory Does distance to the facility reduce CBHI membership? Assumed DAG: wealth and maternal education affect both where households live relative to the facility and whether they join; adjust for both, keep them whatever their p-values (model B, §15.1.2). Report the distance OR, 0.91 per km (recall §13.3).
Predictive Which households should the scheme’s field workers visit first? Pre-specify candidate predictors; fit with shrinkage; judge by discrimination and calibration in new villages (§15.5.2), not by p-values.
Descriptive What share of households in each education group are members? Tabulate 31/168 (18.5%), 50/177 (28.2%), 69/155 (44.5%); no adjustment and no causal claim.

In the explanatory model, a univariable screen at p < 0.05 would have kept distance (crude p < 0.001), wealth (p < 0.001) and education (p < 0.001), and dropped household size (p = 0.56). Here the screen happens to agree with the DAG, but that is a property of this dataset, not of the method: in another dataset a confounder with a weak crude association would be screened out.

points.html: State the aim first. Explanatory → DAG-based adjustment set, one coefficient interpreted. Predictive → accuracy in new data, shrinkage, validation. Descriptive → pre-specified tabulation, association only.
Do not screen variables by univariable p-values (Sun et al., 1996), and do not use stepwise selection to choose confounders (Heinze et al., 2018).

In an explanatory model, do not read the confounders’ coefficients as their effects. They may themselves be confounded, or be direct rather than total effects, even when the exposure’s estimate is not: the “Table 2 fallacy” (Westreich & Greenland, 2013). Interpret the exposure coefficient only.
Keep continuous variables continuous; use splines for curvature (recall §12.4.5).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.2

questions.prompt: A thesis protocol says, “Variables with p < 0.2 in univariable analysis will be entered into a multivariable model, and backward elimination will give the final model of risk factors for low birthweight.” Give two problems, one about each step.
questions.answer: Univariable screening: a confounded risk factor can show no crude association and appear only after adjustment, so the screen can wrongly discard important variables (Sun, Shook & Kay, 1996). Backward elimination: the final model depends on the sample and the criterion, is unstable, and the p-values and CIs of the survivors ignore the selection, so they are too optimistic (Heinze et al., 2018). A better protocol states the aim. For the effect of one exposure, choose the adjustment set from a DAG; for a list of predictors, pre-specify candidates and validate the model.

questions.prompt: For a model predicting which pregnant women will miss their third antenatal visit, is it acceptable to include a variable that is not a cause of missing the visit? Would the same variable be acceptable in a model estimating the effect of ASHA home visits on attendance?
questions.answer: In a predictive model, yes: any variable available at the time of prediction that improves accuracy in new data is acceptable, whether or not it is a cause. In an explanatory model of ASHA visits, not automatically: variables enter because the DAG shows they block backdoor paths. A variable that is a consequence of ASHA visits (a mediator) or a collider must be left out, and one unrelated to the question adds nothing.

questions.prompt: In the CBHI bootstrap of §15.1.3, household size entered 15.5% of the final AIC-selected models. Out of 200 bootstrap samples, how many is that, and what does it tell you about a single stepwise run?
questions.answer: 0.155 × 200 = 31 samples. A variable with no detectable association with membership was selected in about one run in six, so a variable’s presence in a single stepwise model is weak evidence that it matters. Reporting inclusion frequencies shows how much the “final model” depends on the particular sample.
